title: Influence of processing route on microstructure and wear resistance of fly ash reinforced AZ31 magnesium matrix composites

nodes.label: Magnesium alloys are too soft for sliding-contact parts; a cheap reinforcement is needed that actually raises wear resistance
The processing route, not the reinforcement itself, decides the dispersion, the interface and the grain size of a fly-ash/AZ31 composite, and hence its wear behaviour
AZ31B magnesium alloy as the matrix
10 vol.% fly ash, average size about 10 um, as a waste-derived reinforcement whose density is close to that of the melt
The comparison axis is the route itself: conventional stir casting against friction stir processing, same alloy and same 10 vol.% fly ash
Stir casting: AZ31B melted at 720 C, preheated fly ash stirred into the vortex, poured into a preheated mould and solidified under 20 kN
Friction stir processing: fly ash packed in a machined groove in an AZ31 plate, HCHCr tool at 1200 rpm and 40 mm/min, entirely below the melting point

attrs.parameters: 1200 rpm, 40 mm/min, 18 mm shoulder, 6 mm pin

nodes.label: Dry sliding pin-on-disc test (ASTM G99): 20 N, 1.0 m/s, 3000 m sliding distance
Stir casting leaves the fly ash bunched, with fields full of particles and fields with none; FSP scatters it through every section of the stir zone
The cast particles sit in haloes of reaction debris from contact with the 720 C melt; the FSP particles have sharp, debris-free boundaries with the matrix
Grains are coarse in the casting (about 145 um) and fine and equiaxed after FSP (about 4 um)
FSP breaks the hollow fly-ash spheres into angular fragments; the cast particles keep their spherical outline
Microhardness is 94 HV after FSP against 62 HV as cast, a 51% gain
The FSP composite wears about 33% more slowly (280 against 420 x10-5 mm3/m) and with a lower friction coefficient
Both composites wear abrasively, but the casting ploughs into large craters with coarse plate debris while the FSP surface stays grooved with fine debris

attrs.class: abrasive wear; two-body ploughing vs three-body abrasion

nodes.label: Dynamic recrystallisation during FSP refines the grains and the broken particles pin the boundaries, so Hall-Petch and Orowan strengthening both raise the hardness
Evenly spread, well-bonded particles carry the load and their fine debris rolls between the surfaces, so the counterface asperities cut less deeply
Under 20 N dry sliding the FSP composite loses about 240 um of height against 350 um for the casting, with a steady rather than a spiky wear record

attrs.condition: 20 N, 1.0 m/s dry sliding against a steel disc

nodes.label: The route decides the composite: FSP gives homogeneous dispersion, clean interfaces and 4 um grains, and with them higher hardness and a third less wear
Where wear resistance governs, make the fly-ash/AZ31 composite by FSP rather than by stir casting
One composition and one FSP parameter set are compared, and the height-loss record covers only about 1160 s of the nominal 3000 s of sliding
In the cast composite one field is crowded with particles and reaction debris while the next, at the same magnification, holds a single particle over tens of micrometres

attrs.image_note: sizes read against the 20 um bar printed in both panels at X750

nodes.label: SiO2 reflections appear in both composites and are stronger and better defined after FSP
FSP is a hot-working route that refines grains by dynamic recrystallisation and disperses particles by three-dimensional material flow
Hall-Petch hardening with grain refinement and Orowan strengthening by fine dispersed particles
Archard's wear law: wear rate varies inversely with hardness
Fly ash is a waste-derived powder of mainly SiO2 and Al2O3 whose density is close to that of molten magnesium, so it stays suspended
Parallel grooves on a worn surface indicate abrasive wear; smeared and transferred layers indicate the adhesive wear typical of unreinforced magnesium

notes: Two-route comparison: the two PRC nodes are alternatives realized from the same DES/variable_sweep, and each structural node carries both routes' states in one label so the contrast stays on the spine. Lost: Tables 1-3 (alloy and fly-ash compositions, hardness, COF and wear rate), the optical micrographs (F3, F5), the fly-ash feedstock morphology (F1), the XRD (F2) and the misorientation distributions (F8) were not opened, so the hardness and wear-rate numbers enter as a table OBS. Image findings: the height-loss traces cross near 450 s, with the FSP pin wearing faster before that (e10), and the record stops near 1160 s although the stated test is 3000 s long; the cast fly-ash spheres keep their round outline and are ringed by reaction debris rather than having 'lost their shape' (e3); intact cenospheres measure 30-40 um against a stated 10 um feedstock average (e7); only about six grains lie inside the cast EBSD field, so the 145 um average is thinly based (e6); the FSP dispersion is even but not free of clusters or bare patches (e2). Figure defect: in F4 and F6 the printed magnifications and the drawn scale bars are mutually inconsistent, a 20 um bar being almost the same length at 1.0 kX and at 2.0 kX. Panel section: F9 is the only tier-B figure and is offered as a single whole-figure id.

changes: e7: label and image_note corrected - measured against the 30 um bar printed in F4b the intact cenospheres run from about 25 um to roughly 60-70 um for the largest, not 30-40 um. The node's point against the 10 um quoted feedstock size stands and is strengthened.

panel_checks.note: the cast spheres keep clean circular outlines and are ringed by fine debris and bright patches; one broken cenosphere is visible. The node is right that 'many particles lost their shape' is not what this view shows.

the cast IPF map is filled by about six large colour domains (green, periwinkle, orange, red, dark blue, magenta) each wider than the 100 um bar, with roughly a third of the field taken up by multicoloured speckle. e5's companion reading from the same panel is confirmed too.

at 1160 s the stir-cast (red, spiky) trace is at about 350 um and the FSP (blue, smooth) at about 240 um, and the record stops there. e10's crossing is confirmed in the same figure: the blue FSP trace is above red from roughly 50 to 450 s.

review.audit_summary: 4 audits (d22 scope, e6 the six-grain EBSD field, e7 cenosphere size, e10 the early crossing where FSP wears faster). All four change the support of a spine claim, and e10 in particular qualifies the headline wear result fairly: it says the traces cross, not that the result is wrong.
